content: The median, in the context of probability theory and statistics, is defined as the value that separates the higher half of a dataset, population, or probability distribution from the lower half. To determine the median of a finite set of numbers, one must arrange all observations in ascending order and select the middle value. If the dataset contains an even number of observations, the median is not unique, and it is common practice to calculate the mean of the two central values. At most, half of the population will have values less than the median, and at most, half will have values greater than the median. If both groups contain fewer than half of the population, then some members of the population will have values exactly equal to the median. The distinction between the median and the mean can be illustrated with a simple example. Imagine a room with 19 impoverished individuals and one billionaire. If everyone contributes all the money they have, the total amount is £1,000,000,095.75. Dividing this total by the 20 individuals gives a mean of £50,000,004.79. However, the median amount is £5, as the group can be divided into two equal halves, with the first half contributing no more than £5 and the second half contributing no less than £5. In this scenario, the median represents the amount brought in by a typical individual, whereas the mean is heavily influenced by the outlier (the billionaire). In cases where there is an even number of observations and the two middle values differ, the median is not unique. However, at least half of the numbers in the dataset will be less than or equal to either of the two middle values, and at least half will be greater than or equal to either of the two values. Any number between these two middle values can also be considered a median in such cases. When the median is used as a measure of central tendency in descriptive statistics, several measures of variability can accompany it, such as the range, interquartile range, mean absolute deviation, and median absolute deviation. Since the median corresponds to the second quartile, its calculation is closely related to the concept of quartiles. For datasets consisting of integers, the median should also be an integer. In cases where the dataset has an even number of elements, two medians can be identified: the lower median and the upper median. For probability distributions, the median is defined as the value ( m ) that satisfies specific inequalities involving the cumulative distribution function ( F ). For absolutely continuous probability distributions with a probability density function ( f ), the median can be determined using these properties. For specific distributions, the median can be directly estimated from their parameters. For example, the median of a normal distribution with mean ( mu ) and variance ( sigma^2 ) is ( mu ). The median of an exponential distribution with parameter ( lambda ) is ( ln(2)/lambda ). For a Weibull distribution with shape parameter ( k ) and scale parameter ( lambda ), the median is ( (ln(2))^{1/k}/lambda ). The median is particularly useful for skewed distributions, as it provides a measure of central tendency that is less affected by extreme values compared to the arithmetic mean. For example, in the dataset {1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 9}, the median is 2, while the mean is approximately 3.166. The median is a robust statistic, making it a popular choice for summarizing data in the presence of outliers. In probability theory, the median minimizes the expected absolute deviation from a random variable ( X ). However, the median is not always unique and may not be well-defined in all cases. For continuous probability distributions, the difference between the mean and the median is less than or equal to one standard deviation. This relationship is an example of an inequality involving location and scale parameters. Efficient computation of the median is possible even for large datasets. While sorting ( n ) items typically requires ( O(n log n) ) operations, the median can be computed in ( O(n) ) operations using a divide and conquer algorithm. This method can also be used to find the ( k )-th smallest element in a dataset, a problem known as the selection problem.
